chapters.title: Laundry Day at the Inn
chapters.text:
Monday morning brought gray skies and a mountain of washing to the Gull's Rest Inn. Dottie Quill met Hattie at the back door with a sigh as big as the harbor. "Half the guests packed up and left after poor Mr. Crane," she said, "and every one of them left their sheets behind. I could use an extra pair of hands." Hattie was glad to help, though she also hoped to look around a little.

She rolled up her sleeves and followed Dottie into the steamy laundry room, where a big wicker basket sat overflowing beside the machines. Biscuit, who had trotted along uninvited, curled up on a stack of folded towels as if he owned them. The two women sorted pillowcases from tablecloths and chatted about the weather.

Near the bottom of the basket, Hattie's fingers closed on a crumpled kitchen apron. She shook it out. Across the front ran odd green stains, darker than grass and badly smeared, as though someone had wiped their hands in a hurry. "Whose is this?" she asked.

Dottie squinted at it. "Could be anyone's. Rupert keeps a stack by the kitchen for guests who like to help with breakfast. Folks borrow them and toss them back." She reached for the starch. "Why, does it matter?"

"Probably not," said Hattie lightly. But when Dottie turned away, she slipped out her little green notebook and wrote down the date, the color of the stains, and the faint leafy smell that clung to the cotton.

chapters.title: An Innkeeper's Worries
chapters.text:
On Tuesday Hattie carried a basket of blueberry muffins up the inn's front steps, telling herself it was simply the neighborly thing to do. Rupert Ashby sat in his cramped little office behind the front desk, his reading glasses pushed up into his silver hair and a mug of coffee gone cold at his elbow.

The desk was buried in envelopes. Several wore bright red stamps that said PAST DUE, and one from the bank had been opened, read, and crumpled. Rupert swept them into a drawer when he saw her, but not quite fast enough. "Muffins," he said, managing a smile. "You are a kind woman, Hattie Bramble."

She sat down without being asked, a trick she had learned in thirty years of teaching. Before long the whole story tumbled out. The roof leaked, the boiler groaned, and bookings had been thin since spring. "And then Lionel Crane strolls in," Rupert said bitterly, "and offers to buy the place. My grandfather built this inn, and that man offered me a fraction of what it is worth. Said I would be lucky to get it."

"What did you tell him?" Hattie asked gently. Rupert rubbed his eyes. "I told him I would think about it. Well, that offer is gone now, isn't it?" He heard his own words and winced. "That came out wrong."

Hattie patted his hand and said nothing at all, but on the walk home she wrote the word debt in her notebook and underlined it twice.

chapters.title: Old Scorecards
chapters.text:
The harbor smelled of salt, diesel, and frying clams when Hattie walked down to the docks on Wednesday afternoon. Gulls wheeled over the lobster boats, and old Abe Tolliver sat mending a net on an upturned crate. He tipped his cap. "Gordon's in the office," he said, "grumpy as a wet cat."

Gordon Pike was indeed in the harbor office, surrounded by tide charts and a radio that crackled with boat chatter. As chairman of the bake-off committee, he had been run ragged all week, and his ruddy face looked tired. Hattie set a paper bag of ginger cookies on his desk and told him she was putting together a little scrapbook about the history of the Harvest Bake-Off.

"That's nice," Gordon said, reaching for a cookie. "I thought I might borrow the old scorecards," Hattie went on. "The ones from years past, with all the judges' notes. It would be such fun to see who won what." Gordon's hand stopped halfway to his mouth. The cookie snapped in two, and crumbs scattered over a tide chart.

"Those are long gone," he said quickly. "Thrown out. Water damage. Ages ago." He brushed at the crumbs far longer than they needed. "Nobody cares about old scores, Hattie. Best leave them be."

Hattie thanked him and wandered back up the hill, thinking hard. In her experience, people rarely got that flustered over paperwork they truly did not care about.

chapters.title: A Taste He Hated
chapters.text:
Deputy Sam Bramble came into the Rolling Pin on Thursday morning looking as though he had not slept in a week. Hattie poured him a mug of strong coffee and set a warm cinnamon roll in front of him before he could even say hello. Biscuit wound around his boots, purring hopefully.

"Detective Hask has me running in circles," Sam groaned between bites. "Forms, phone calls, more forms. And the lab results are just plain strange. They tested that fancy teacup of his, the one with his initials on it. Traces of honey, they said. Honey and tea, as far as they can tell so far." He froze, his roll halfway to his mouth. "Aunt Hattie, forget I said that. I am not supposed to talk about the case."

Hattie mimed zipping her lips, but her mind was already racing. She remembered an old episode of Lionel's cooking show, where he had wrinkled his famous nose at a jar of clover honey. "The sticky crutch of lazy bakers," he had called it. He had refused it in his tea for twenty years and told anyone who would listen. Every food magazine in the country had printed that line.

"Sam," she said slowly, "why would a man who hated honey drink it in his tea?" Sam shrugged and reached for another napkin. "Maybe he changed his mind."

Hattie doubted it very much. Men like Lionel Crane did not change their minds about anything, least of all their own tea.

chapters.title: The Painter by the Light
chapters.text:
On Friday afternoon the bell over the bakery door jingled, and in walked Imogen Vale with paint on her fingers and a canvas bag over one shoulder. She was tall and windblown, with a long red scarf wrapped twice around her neck. She ordered a cup of chamomile and a slice of apple pie and chose the little table by the window.

Hattie brought the pie over herself. "I'm so sorry about your uncle," she said. Imogen gave a short laugh that was not really a laugh. "Thank you. Though we hadn't spoken in nine years. He told me painting was a hobby for people with no talent." She stirred her tea. "I suppose you've heard I get his house. And his savings. The whole village seems to know."

"Villages do talk," Hattie admitted. Imogen nodded. "Well, let them. I was up at the lighthouse that morning, painting the sunrise over the rocks, same as every clear day. I didn't even know he'd collapsed until supper." She pulled a small sketchbook from her bag and flipped it open to a watercolor of the lighthouse, pink and gold against the sea.

It was lovely, Hattie thought. It was also unsigned and undated, and anyone could paint a sunrise on any morning at all. Biscuit hopped onto the empty chair and sniffed at the paint on Imogen's sleeve.

After she left, Hattie jotted down the hours Imogen claimed to have been painting. Then, after a moment, she added a small question mark.

chapters.title: Lost and Found
chapters.text:
Dottie Quill kept the lost-and-found box in a cupboard under the front stairs, and on Saturday morning she hauled it out with a grunt. "Detective Hask wants it all logged," she told Hattie, "and my eyes aren't what they were. Would you mind reading things off while I write?"

Hattie did not mind one bit. The box held the usual odds and ends of a seaside inn. There was a single leather glove, a pair of sunglasses, a child's plastic shovel, three umbrellas, a paperback with a cracked spine, and a hairbrush nobody would ever claim. Biscuit climbed straight into the box and sat on the umbrellas, purring like a little engine.

Tucked inside the paperback, marking a page, was a torn train ticket stub. Hattie held it up to the window. Boston to Portland, it read, one adult, and it was stamped with a date she knew at once. It was the day before the bake-off guests were due to arrive. Every visitor for the contest, Lionel's party included, had checked in together on the same afternoon. Hattie remembered it clearly, because she had delivered the welcome scones.

"Someone got here early," she murmured. Dottie peered over her glasses. "Or someone came and went. Folks drop things in that box from all over, Hattie. Could be from last month's guests, for all I know."

Hattie copied the date carefully into her notebook. Somebody, it seemed, had been in Pennywhistle Harbor a day sooner than anyone had said.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Tea
chapters.text:
Hattie found Colette Marsh on the inn's back porch late Sunday afternoon, wrapped in a gray cardigan and staring out at the garden. A cup of tea sat untouched on the rail beside her. She looked smaller than ever, Hattie thought, like a sparrow that had lost its flock.

"May I sit?" Hattie asked, and Colette nodded. Then Colette said softly, "Twelve years. I worked for him for twelve years. I knew exactly how he liked everything. Darjeeling, steeped four minutes, the cup warmed first. Never milk, never sugar. I typed his columns, answered his letters, and tested his recipes until midnight." She smiled faintly. "People thought he was cruel. He could be. But he was my whole job, my whole life."

Hattie gently asked where she had been on the morning of the bake-off. Colette did not seem to mind the question. "At the library," she said. "Lionel wanted a stack of old regional cookbooks for his research, so I went to fetch them first thing. By the time I reached the green, it was all over." Her voice wobbled, and she dabbed her eyes with a folded handkerchief.

Hattie squeezed her hand. Biscuit, who had followed her up the steps, settled against Colette's ankle, and she stroked him absently with neat, careful fingers. The garden rustled in the cool breeze below them.

That evening Hattie wrote down every word, the way she wrote down everything, and wondered what twelve years of loyalty might feel like.

chapters.title: Recipes in the Margins
chapters.text:
Monday morning was the busiest the Rolling Pin had seen all week. Half the village seemed to want pumpkin bread, and a cluster of guests from the Gull's Rest Inn crowded in for coffee before their trains home. Hattie rang up orders until her feet ached, and Biscuit wisely hid under the counter.

When the rush finally ended, she found a worn leather notebook left behind on the table by the window. It had no name inside the cover, only page after page of handwritten recipes in faded blue ink. Maple walnut tart. Cranberry orange scones. A brown butter pound cake with a pinch of cardamom. The margins were crowded with tiny notes like "less salt" and "bake five minutes longer" and "try with lemon zest."

Something tugged at Hattie's memory. She fetched her own copy of Lionel Crane's famous cookbook from the shelf behind the register, the one with his smug photograph on the cover. She turned the pages slowly, then turned them again. The maple walnut tart was there, word for word. So were the scones and the pound cake, right down to the cardamom.

Hattie sat very still. Either someone had copied Lionel's recipes into a notebook by hand, with years of careful notes in the margins, or the recipes had been written here first.

She wrapped the notebook in a clean tea towel and tucked it safely behind the counter. Whoever had left it would surely come back for it, and she meant to return it herself.

chapters.title: A Nasty Note
chapters.text:
Tuesday dawned cold and bright, and Hattie was halfway through her first batch of croissants when Winnie Calloway rapped on the bakery's back door. "You had better come," Winnie said, pulling her shawl tight. "It's Delia."

Across the square, a small crowd had gathered outside the Sugar and Spoon. Taped to the front window was a sheet of paper with a single cruel word printed in thick black marker, followed by a line telling Delia to pack up and leave town. Delia Fairweather stood on the sidewalk in her flour-dusted smock, arms folded tight, chin trembling. "I have baked for this village for six years," she said quietly. "Six years, and now this."

Hattie did not waste a moment. She marched back for a bucket of warm soapy water, two sponges, and a bottle of vinegar for the sticky tape. Winnie brought three mugs of cocoa from her bookshop and handed them round. The crowd, a little ashamed, began to drift away. Together the three women peeled and scrubbed until the glass sparkled and not a scrap remained.

Before she threw the paper away, Hattie folded it neatly and slipped it into her coat pocket. The printing was careful and blocky, the sort of hand someone uses when they do not want their writing known. "Whoever did this," she told Delia firmly, "is a coward. And cowards make mistakes."

Delia managed a watery smile and wrapped both hands around her cocoa. "Then I hope you catch one, Hattie."

chapters.title: Biscuit Knocks a Jar
chapters.text:
Wednesday night the bakery was warm and quiet, and Hattie was mixing a double batch of spice cake for the church supper. The radio hummed softly, the oven ticked as it heated, and Biscuit prowled along the top of the shelves where he was not allowed to be.

She had just set the kitchen timer when she heard a clink, a wobble, and a crash. A glass jar of nutmeg had rolled off the shelf and burst on the floor, scattering brown powder from the sink to the pantry. Biscuit peered down at the mess innocently. "You rascal," Hattie scolded, reaching for the broom. The kitchen filled with a warm, sharp fragrance.

As she swept, Hattie thought about spice cake. Nobody tasted the nutmeg the moment it went into the bowl. The flavor bloomed slowly, in the oven, long after the mixing was done. By the time the timer rang, the real work had happened an hour before. The timer only told you when to look.

She stopped sweeping. Everyone in the village had watched Lionel bite into Delia's plum cake and collapse soon after, so naturally they all blamed the cake. But what if the cake was only the timer ringing? What if the trouble had begun much earlier that morning, in a place where nobody was watching?

Hattie leaned the broom against the counter and reached for her green notebook. Biscuit hopped down, rubbed against her ankles, and purred as if he had planned it all along.
